night.Japanese_action: No fortress-wide banzai. Three to five local infiltration/counterattack packets use debris, vegetation and surviving phone/runner cells to probe Marine seams, mortar/artillery observation posts and supply routes. The largest dawn packet is roughly 80-120 men; total participants over the night are about 200-280, not simultaneous.
night.local_success: One or two penetrations reach roughly 70-130 m into forward positions or support lanes and cause temporary 20-40 minute local disruption. No durable severing of the beachhead or artillery support network.
night.US_response: Pre-registered 75/105-mm defensive fires, star-shell illumination, machine guns, tanks held behind the line, and short destroyer/LCI(G) fire missions. US commanders meter illumination and artillery because friendly lines are close.
night.dawn_state: Japanese organized/local fighters about 500-690, plus 260-390 scattered/support personnel capable of local defense.

daylight_7Feb.result: Roi pockets are reduced in the morning. On Namur, tank/engineer/direct-fire teams work north and east strongpoint by strongpoint. Better shelters and local ammunition keep some positions alive after suppression, but lack of depth and loss of island-wide C2 make mutual support increasingly impossible.
daylight_7Feb.support_shift: As Roi mopping ends, tanks/fire-support teams can reinforce Namur. This does not happen instantaneously; causeway/landing-craft movement and rubble create a morning transition lag.
daylight_7Feb.T24_remaining: About 110-190 isolated/local fighters plus 70-130 scattered/support personnel; no coherent island-level counterattack capability.

assessment: Stronger Branch defenses prolong Namur into late D+1, but removal of the historical large torpedo-magazine catastrophe and very strong US registered fires/tank-engineer reduction prevent a simple one-way casualty inflation.
